newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs snub Senate poll again despite Havel appeal.
newsitem.headline: Czechs snub Senate poll again despite Havel appeal.

text.p: Czechs voted in run-offs for a new Senate on Saturday amid signs that few had heeded President Vaclav Havel's appeal for a bigger turnout following widespread apathy in last weekend's first round.
Election officials estimated that turnout in the second round held on Friday and Saturday had been about the same or a little higher than the 35 percent on November 15 and 16.

Voter apathy is likely to benefit the well-funded and organised Civic Democratic Party (ODS) of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus which was successful in getting its supporters, shocked when the coalition government lost its majority in lower house polls in June, to vote in the first round.
But the low turnout also threw into question whether Klaus could regain his majority by achieving the same performance in lower house polls, where participation is usually far higher.

ODS won 36.5 percent compared with 20.3 percent for the opposition Social Democrats, whose leader Milos Zeman came close to admitting defeat even before the second round ended at 2 pm (1300 GMT) on Saturday.
Zeman blamed a rift in the party's ranks after four rebel deputies voted with the Klaus government in a parliamentary budget vote last month.
"We can fail to succeed in the Senate elections simply because we sometimes don't manage to find a united approach to important matters," he told the Prague daily Mlada Fronta Dnes.

One of the rebels, party deputy chairman Karel Machovec, retaliated by blaming Zeman's scepticism about the very need for an upper house of parliament. "We were harmed by his statements that the Senate is useless and that if we succeed in the elections we'll abolish it anyway," said Machovec.
The Social Democrats have said they would scrap the Senate if they ever achieved the three-fifths majority in the lower Chamber of Deputies needed to change the constitution.

Scepticism is widespread among Czechs and Klaus himself has questioned the need for the Senate, which was written into the Czech Republic's new constitution when Czechoslovakia split at the end of 1992, but is only now being elected.
Klaus toned down his scepticism as voting neared but only Havel has appeared enthusiastic about the idea.

Before the run-offs -- for the top two first round candidates in constituencies where no one won more than half the vote -- Havel appealed to citizens to turn out in much greater numbers for the sake of the Senate's legitimacy.
But a poll commissioned by Czech Television showed that things were unlikely to be any better.
The poll, taken on Thursday, showed that 48 percent of respondents had declared their intention to vote.
But Petr Mateju of the SC&C agency which took the poll said that actual turnout was traditionally lower than the declared level and he forecast it would be again around 35 percent.

Results from the 71 constituencies being contested -- four candidates won outright in the first round -- are expected to start running at about 5 pm (1600 GMT) with full results known around midnight (2300 GMT.
